Define monitoring frequencies for each control type and document them. Feed monitoring results into the risk assessment and POA&M. Assessors will review the monitoring program structure, look at monitoring outputs and evidence of regular review, and verify the defined frequencies. Organizations that conduct annual point-in-time assessments only — with no ongoing monitoring between assessments — do not satisfy this control.

3.12.4.title: System Security Plan
3.12.4.summary: Develop, document, and periodically update system security plans that describe system boundaries, system environments of operation, how security requirements are implemented, and the relationships with or connections to other systems.
3.12.4.requirement: Develop, document, and periodically update system security plans that describe system boundaries, system environments of operation, how security requirements are implemented, and the relationships with or connections to other systems.
3.12.4.onboarding_tips: Develop and maintain a System Security Plan (SSP) that accurately describes the system boundary, CUI data flows, the operational environment, and the current implementation status of all 110 CMMC Level 2 controls. The SSP must reflect actual configurations and practices — not aspirational or planned states. Review and update the SSP at least annually and whenever significant system changes occur. Assessors will compare SSP control implementation statements against observed system configurations and practices throughout the assessment. SSP statements that claim controls are 'implemented' when they are not, or describe configurations that do not match observed reality, directly undermine the assessment and can result in serious findings.

3.13.1.title: Boundary Protection [CUI Data]
3.13.1.requirement: Monitor, control, and protect communications (i.e., information transmitted or received by organizational systems) at the external boundaries and key internal boundaries of organizational systems.
3.13.1.onboarding_tips: Define and document a clear system boundary. Implement boundary protection — firewall, next-generation firewall, proxy — to monitor and control all traffic at the boundary between the CUI environment and other networks. Implement network segmentation using VLANs, subnets, and firewall rules to isolate CUI systems from general-purpose networks. Enforce traffic policies based on deny-all/permit-by-exception. Assessors will review firewall configurations, boundary diagrams, and network architecture. Overly permissive firewall rules, poorly defined system boundaries, and no network segmentation between CUI systems and general business systems are common findings.

3.13.2.title: Security Engineering
3.13.2.summary: Employ architectural designs, software development techniques, and systems engineering principles that promote effective information security within organizational systems.
3.13.2.requirement: Employ architectural designs, software development techniques, and systems engineering principles that promote effective information security within organizational systems.
3.13.2.onboarding_tips: Apply security engineering principles during the development, acquisition, implementation, and modification of CUI systems: defense in depth, least privilege, fail-secure defaults, separation of functions, and minimizing the attack surface. Require security review as part of all system change and procurement processes. Maintain system architecture documentation that reflects security design decisions. Assessors will review architecture documentation and assess whether security was considered systematically during design and change. Organizations that deploy systems based on vendor recommendations without any security engineering review, and with no architecture documentation, struggle with this control.

3.13.3.title: Role Separation
3.13.3.summary: Separate user functionality from system management functionality.
3.13.3.requirement: Separate user functionality from system management functionality.
3.13.3.onboarding_tips: Separate user functionality from security management functionality at a technical level — users must not be able to access or modify security controls, audit configurations, or security management interfaces. Administrative interfaces must be separately authenticated and access-controlled. For web applications, the administrative interface must be completely separate from the user-facing interface with its own authentication path. Assessors will verify that standard users cannot reach security management functions and that admin interfaces are separately protected. Web application administrative panels reachable from the same user-facing URL path with insufficient access controls are a critical finding.

3.13.4.title: Shared Resource Control
3.13.4.summary: Prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources.
3.13.4.requirement: Prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources.
3.13.4.onboarding_tips: Implement mechanisms that prevent unauthorized information transfer between shared system resources — ensuring one process cannot read memory or storage allocated to another, and that storage is cleared before reallocation. In virtualization environments, verify VMs cannot access resources allocated to other VMs. For shared cloud environments, validate tenant isolation configurations. Apply to shared workstations, multi-tenant database instances, and any shared computing resource in the CUI environment. Assessors will review virtualization and cloud isolation configurations. Incorrectly configured virtualization hypervisors allowing cross-VM resource access are a finding in virtualized CUI environments.

3.13.5.title: Public-Access System Separation [CUI Data]
3.13.5.summary: Implement subnetworks for publicly accessible system components that are physically or logically separated from internal networks.
3.13.5.requirement: Implement subnetworks for publicly accessible system components that are physically or logically separated from internal networks.
3.13.5.onboarding_tips: Place publicly accessible systems (web servers, email gateways, VPN concentrators) in a dedicated DMZ that is isolated from internal networks containing CUI. CUI systems must never be directly accessible from the internet. Use firewalls to restrict DMZ-to-internal traffic to the minimum required flows. Document the DMZ architecture in your network boundary diagrams. Assessors will review network diagrams and verify DMZ implementation with firewall rule examination. Finding web servers or externally accessible systems co-located on the same network segment as workstations or servers that process CUI is a common architectural finding.

3.13.6.title: Network Communication By Exception
3.13.6.summary: Deny network communications traffic by default and allow network communications traffic by exception (i.
3.13.6.requirement: Deny network communications traffic by default and allow network communications traffic by exception (i.e., deny all, permit by exception).
3.13.6.onboarding_tips: Implement a deny-all, permit-by-exception firewall posture for all network communications. Configure all firewalls, security groups, and routing policy to deny traffic by default and explicitly permit only what is necessary and documented. Regularly review and remove stale, overly broad, or undocumented firewall rules. Maintain a firewall rule change log aligned with your change management process. Assessors will review firewall and security group rule sets looking for overly permissive rules (allow any/any), undocumented rules with no business justification, and the absence of a default-deny rule at the end of the policy.

3.13.7.title: Split Tunneling
3.13.7.summary: Prevent remote devices from simultaneously establishing non-remote connections with organizational systems and communicating via some other connection to resources in external networks (i.
3.13.7.requirement: Prevent remote devices from simultaneously establishing non-remote connections with organizational systems and communicating via some other connection to resources in external networks (i.e., split tunneling).
3.13.7.onboarding_tips: Configure VPN and remote access systems to use full-tunnel mode so all traffic from remote endpoints routes through organizational infrastructure before going to any destination. Full-tunnel VPN ensures remote worker traffic is subject to the same monitoring, filtering, and logging as on-site users. Document the VPN configuration and confirm no split-tunnel exceptions exist. Assessors will inspect VPN configuration files and test a live remote session to verify routing behavior. Split-tunnel VPN configurations — where only internal traffic routes through the VPN — are one of the most common findings for this control.

3.13.8.title: Data In Transit
3.13.8.summary: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure of CUI during transmission unless otherwise protected by alternative physical safeguards.
3.13.8.requirement: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure of CUI during transmission unless otherwise protected by alternative physical safeguards.
3.13.8.onboarding_tips: Protect all CUI transmitted over external networks using FIPS-validated cryptographic mechanisms. All web portals and APIs handling CUI must use TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites. Email with CUI must be encrypted using S/MIME, PGP, or a secure email gateway. File transfers must use SFTP, FTPS, or HTTPS. Disable deprecated protocols: SSL, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and weak cipher suites (RC4, DES, 3DES). Assessors will run protocol analysis on all external-facing services (use SSL Labs for web services) and inspect email and file transfer configurations. Legacy protocols and weak cipher suites remaining enabled are among the most common technical findings.

3.13.9.title: Connections Termination
3.13.9.summary: Terminate network connections associated with communications sessions at the end of the sessions or after a defined period of inactivity.
3.13.9.requirement: Terminate network connections associated with communications sessions at the end of the sessions or after a defined period of inactivity.
3.13.9.onboarding_tips: Configure idle timeout and session termination for all network connections involving CUI: application sessions, database connections, management interfaces, and network sessions on firewalls and switches. Define and enforce maximum session durations for each connection type. Sessions must terminate — not merely lock — after the defined idle period. Assessors will verify idle connection timeout settings across network devices, application servers, and database configurations. Infinite timeouts on database connections, management console sessions, and application programming interfaces are common findings in security control reviews.

3.13.10.title: Key Management
3.13.10.summary: Establish and manage cryptographic keys for cryptography employed in organizational systems.
3.13.10.requirement: Establish and manage cryptographic keys for cryptography employed in organizational systems.
3.13.10.onboarding_tips: Establish and implement cryptographic key management policies and procedures covering the full key lifecycle: generation (using approved RNGs), storage (HSM or encrypted key vault), distribution (secure channels only), rotation (defined schedule), and destruction (certified wiping or physical destruction). Use a dedicated Key Management System or Hardware Security Module for high-value keys. Document all keys in use, their purpose, custodians, and rotation schedule. Assessors will review key management procedures and examine key storage implementations. Cryptographic keys stored in plaintext configuration files, spreadsheets, or code repositories are a critical finding.

3.13.11.title: CUI Encryption
3.13.11.summary: Employ FIPS-validated cryptography when used to protect the confidentiality of CUI.
3.13.11.requirement: Employ FIPS-validated cryptography when used to protect the confidentiality of CUI.
3.13.11.onboarding_tips: Implement FIPS 140-2 or 140-3 validated cryptographic modules for all encryption protecting CUI — this means using modules that have completed NIST validation testing, not merely using AES algorithmically. For Windows environments, enable FIPS-compliant algorithms via Group Policy. For cloud services, select services documented as using FIPS-validated modules. For custom applications, use FIPS-validated cryptographic libraries. Maintain a record of FIPS-validated modules in use across the environment. Assessors will verify the FIPS validation status of cryptographic implementations. Using AES algorithmically through a library that has not completed FIPS 140 validation is technically non-compliant.

3.13.12.title: Collaborative Device Control
3.13.12.summary: Prohibit remote activation of collaborative computing devices and provide indication of devices in use to users present at the device.
3.13.12.requirement: Prohibit remote activation of collaborative computing devices and provide indication of devices in use to users present at the device.
3.13.12.onboarding_tips: Implement controls for collaborative computing devices — cameras, microphones, smart speakers, and interactive whiteboards — in spaces where CUI is discussed or processed. Physical controls: camera covers, microphone mute policies, and clear-room policies for sensitive discussions. For remote collaboration tools used with CUI, approve and vet the tools, configure them for enterprise security (E2E encryption, controlled recording), and prohibit use of consumer-grade personal accounts. Assessors will review the collaborative computing policy and associated physical controls. The most common finding is no policy governing video conferencing tools for CUI discussions, or use of consumer-grade tools without enterprise security assessment.

3.13.13.title: Mobile Code
3.13.13.summary: Control and monitor the use of mobile code.
3.13.13.requirement: Control and monitor the use of mobile code.
3.13.13.onboarding_tips: Implement controls on the use of mobile code — JavaScript, scripts, applets — on systems processing CUI. Implement Content Security Policy (CSP) headers on all web applications to restrict script execution to approved sources. Configure browsers on CUI systems to restrict or control script execution from untrusted sources. Document the policy governing acceptable mobile code sources and the technical controls enforcing it. Assessors will review web application security headers, browser configuration policies, and mobile code use policies. Web applications lacking CSP headers and allowing script execution from arbitrary third-party CDN sources are common findings.

3.13.14.title: Voice Over Internet Protocol
3.13.14.summary: Control and monitor the use of Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) technologies.
3.13.14.requirement: Control and monitor the use of Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) technologies.
3.13.14.onboarding_tips: Assess and manage VoIP system security in CUI environments. Segment VoIP traffic on a dedicated VLAN isolated from data networks. Encrypt VoIP signaling using TLS-protected SIP and media using SRTP. Manage VoIP endpoints as managed devices with firmware update programs and hardened configurations. Assess VoIP infrastructure for vulnerabilities as part of your regular vulnerability management program. Assessors will review VoIP network architecture and security configurations. VoIP and data traffic sharing a flat network without VLAN segmentation, and unencrypted SIP traffic in environments containing CUI, are common findings.

3.13.15.title: Communications Authenticity
3.13.15.summary: Protect the authenticity of communications sessions.
3.13.15.requirement: Protect the authenticity of communications sessions.
3.13.15.onboarding_tips: Authenticate communications sessions involving CUI to verify communicating parties and protect against message tampering. Use authenticated protocols: TLS for web and API communications, SSH for remote management, STARTTLS/SMTPS for email. Avoid unauthenticated communication protocols for any CUI exchange — no plain FTP, plain HTTP, or unauthenticated SMTP for CUI. Implement certificate validation and mutual TLS (mTLS) for high-sensitivity system-to-system communications. Assessors will inspect communications protocols used for CUI systems and verify session authentication is in place. Unauthenticated file transfer (plain FTP) and plaintext HTTP used for CUI are common findings.

3.13.16.title: Data At Rest
3.13.16.summary: Protect the confidentiality of CUI at rest.
3.13.16.requirement: Protect the confidentiality of CUI at rest.
3.13.16.onboarding_tips: Encrypt CUI at rest across all storage systems: servers, workstations, databases, NAS/SAN, and backup media. Implement Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) or column-level encryption for databases containing CUI. Use BitLocker (Windows, with TPM), FileVault (macOS), or LUKS (Linux) for system drives. Encrypt backup media at the software or hardware level. Document the encryption implementation for each CUI storage location in your SSP. Assessors will verify encryption on all CUI storage systems identified during boundary scoping. CUI found in unencrypted databases, flat file shares, or on unencrypted workstation drives is one of the most universally cited findings in CMMC assessments.

3.14.1.title: Flaw Remediation [CUI Data]
3.14.1.summary: Identify, report, and correct system flaws in a timely manner.
3.14.1.requirement: Identify, report, and correct system flaws in a timely manner.
3.14.1.onboarding_tips: Identify, report, and remediate software flaws and security vulnerabilities on a defined, risk-based schedule: critical within 14–30 days, high within 60 days, medium within 90 days. Apply patches to all components: operating systems, applications, firmware, network devices, and security appliances — not only server OS. Document the patch management process with defined timelines, responsibilities, and tracking mechanisms. Assessors will compare vulnerability scan results against patch deployment records and will test systems for known unpatched vulnerabilities. Finding critical vulnerabilities months old on CUI systems is one of the most common and impactful findings in CMMC Level 2 assessments.

3.14.2.title: Malicious Code Protection [CUI Data]
3.14.2.summary: Provide protection from malicious code at designated locations within organizational systems.
3.14.2.requirement: Provide protection from malicious code at designated locations within organizational systems.
3.14.2.onboarding_tips: Deploy endpoint detection and response (EDR) or antimalware on all workstations, servers, and endpoints that access CUI. Protection must be active, updated to current signatures, and configured for real-time on-access scanning. Use centralized management so administrators can verify protection status across all endpoints. Configure automatic remediation and quarantine for detected threats. Assessors will inspect endpoint protection on representative systems, verify real-time protection is enabled and signatures are current, and review the central management console. Systems with protection installed but disabled, expired signatures, or protection not deployed uniformly across all CUI endpoints are common findings.

3.14.3.title: Security Alerts & Advisories
3.14.3.summary: Monitor system security alerts and advisories and take action in response.
3.14.3.requirement: Monitor system security alerts and advisories and take action in response.
3.14.3.onboarding_tips: Establish a formal process for receiving, reviewing, and acting on security alerts and advisories from US-CERT, vendor security bulletins, DoD advisories, and relevant ISACs. Designate a named individual responsible for monitoring these sources on a defined schedule. Document how advisories are evaluated for applicability to your environment and how findings are translated into action items, vulnerability scan tasks, or POA&M entries. Assessors will ask who is responsible for advisory monitoring, review documentation of the advisory intake process, and request evidence of recent advisory review cycles. Organizations without a formal advisory monitoring process — relying on ad-hoc discovery — have a gap.

3.14.4.title: Update Malicious Code Protection [CUI Data]
3.14.4.summary: Update malicious code protection mechanisms when new releases are available.
3.14.4.requirement: Update malicious code protection mechanisms when new releases are available.
3.14.4.onboarding_tips: Configure endpoint protection to update signatures automatically and at minimum daily. For cloud-based or AI/ML-driven protection platforms, ensure cloud lookup and threat intelligence feeds are enabled. Do not allow update delays or stale signatures on any CUI endpoint. Implement monitoring in the central management console to alert on endpoints with protection out of date by more than 24 hours. Assessors will inspect signature update dates on representative endpoints via the management console. Systems with signatures more than a few days old, or update checks blocked by network or proxy configuration, are findings.

3.14.5.title: System & File Scanning [CUI Data]
3.14.5.summary: Perform periodic scans of organizational systems and real-time scans of files from external sources as files are downloaded, opened, or executed.
3.14.5.requirement: Perform periodic scans of organizational systems and real-time scans of files from external sources as files are downloaded, opened, or executed.
3.14.5.onboarding_tips: Configure malicious code protection to perform on-access (real-time) scanning for all file system operations on CUI systems. Schedule full-system scans at minimum weekly. Implement email gateway scanning for malicious attachments and links. For web access, deploy proxy-based or DNS-based content filtering. Review scan logs and quarantine activity on a regular schedule. Assessors will verify on-access scanning is enabled, scheduled full scans are configured and completing successfully, and scan/quarantine logs are reviewed. Real-time scanning enabled but periodic full scans never scheduled or consistently failing to complete is a common configuration finding.

3.14.6.title: Monitor Communications For Attacks
3.14.6.summary: Monitor organizational systems, including inbound and outbound communications traffic, to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks.
3.14.6.requirement: Monitor organizational systems, including inbound and outbound communications traffic, to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks.
3.14.6.onboarding_tips: Monitor network communications involving CUI systems for attack indicators and anomalous activity. Implement network-based IDS/IPS at key ingress/egress points and critical internal network segments. Analyze network flow data for behavioral anomalies. Configure EDR behavioral detection for endpoint-level attack indicators. Define and document the monitoring coverage in your SSP. Assign named responsibility for reviewing alerts. Assessors will review IDS/IPS configurations, network monitoring coverage, alert review processes, and coverage documentation. Having a firewall with no traffic inspection beyond basic ACL filtering — no IDS/IPS, no flow analysis — is a common gap.

3.14.7.title: Identify Unauthorized Use
3.14.7.summary: Identify unauthorized use of organizational systems.
3.14.7.requirement: Identify unauthorized use of organizational systems.
3.14.7.onboarding_tips: Implement technical capability to detect unauthorized use of CUI systems beyond basic access control. Deploy behavioral monitoring via UEBA tools or SIEM-based anomaly detection configured with user baselines. Define normal access patterns for key user populations and configure alerts for deviations: after-hours access, access from new locations, bulk data downloads, access to resources outside normal job scope. Review behavioral alerts on a defined schedule. Assessors will ask how the organization would detect unauthorized system use and look for technical evidence of behavioral monitoring capability. Organizations that rely solely on reactive investigation of user reports — with no proactive behavioral monitoring — do not satisfy this control.
